tool.name: React
tool.tagline: Component-based JavaScript library for building user interfaces
tool.description: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components that describe what the screen should show for the current data. It powers web apps through react-dom and frameworks like Next.js and React Router, and native apps through React Native. React 19 adds Actions, the use() API, Server Components and the React Compiler.

glossary.def: In React, to call your components to work out what the screen should show for the current data. React then changes the page only where the result differs. A re-render is doing this again after data changes.
A reusable piece of a React screen: a function whose name starts with a capital letter and that returns JSX describing what to show, like <Avatar /> or <Header />.
How components nest inside each other, like a family tree: App contains a Header and a Feed, the Feed contains Posts, and so on.

HTML-like tags written directly inside JavaScript, such as

Hi

. A build tool turns each tag into an ordinary JavaScript function call before the browser runs the code.
The inputs a component receives from the component that uses it, written like HTML attributes (<Avatar size={48} />) and collected into one object.
A wrapper, written <>...</>, that groups several elements so a component can return them together without adding an extra element to the page.

A special React function whose name starts with use, such as useState, that lets a component keep state or use other React features. Hooks must be called at the top level of a component, never inside if statements or loops.
Your own function whose name starts with use and that calls other Hooks, so several components can reuse the same logic. Each component that calls it gets its own separate state.
React mounts a component when it first adds it to the screen, and unmounts it when it removes it, throwing away its state.
A popular build tool for web apps: while you work it runs your app on your own computer and updates it as you save; for publishing it bundles your code into finished files.
The package manager that comes with Node.js: the command you use to download JavaScript packages into a project and to run the project's commands, as in npm run dev.
JavaScript with type labels added, such as name: string, that a checker reads to catch mistakes before the code runs. It is turned into plain JavaScript to run.
React's way of updating a running app in the browser as soon as you save a file, while keeping what was on screen, such as text you typed.
A form field whose value comes from React state and changes only through an onChange handler. An uncontrolled input instead keeps its own value, which you read when you need it.
A React development helper, <StrictMode>, that runs some of your code twice on purpose to expose bugs from impure components or missing cleanup. It does nothing in the published app.
Code a component runs with useEffect after React updates the page, to keep something outside React (a connection, a timer, a browser feature) in step with the component.
The list of values passed as the last argument to useEffect, useMemo or useCallback. React re-runs the code only when one of those values has changed since the last render.
A function an Effect returns to undo what it set up, such as closing a connection. React calls it before running the Effect again and when the component is removed.
A box made with useRef whose .current value you can change without causing a re-render. Often used to get hold of a page element, for example to focus an input.
A way to draw part of a component somewhere else on the page, such as at the end of <body>, while React still treats it as a child of that component. Used for pop-up dialogs and tooltips.
React's way for a component to make a value available to every component below it, however deep, without passing it through props at each level.
The component, written <SomeContext value={...}>, that supplies a context value to everything inside it.
Passing props down through several layers of components that don't use them, only so a deeply nested component can get them.
Moving state out of two sibling components into their closest shared parent, which then passes the value and a way to change it down to both.
A function that takes the current state and an action describing what happened, and returns the next state without changing the old one. Used with useReducer.
Choosing what to show based on the URL. In a React app, a router picks which screen to display for the current address; on a server, it picks which code handles a request.
React's process of comparing the new description of the screen with the previous one to work out the smallest set of page changes.
The step after rendering in which React actually applies the changes to the page. It always runs to the end in one go, so users never see a half-updated screen.
Checking two sets of values one by one, treating an object as unchanged only if it is the very same object, without looking inside it.
An add-on for your build tool that analyses your components and adds memoization (reusing earlier results) automatically, so you rarely need to do it by hand.
A browser extension for inspecting React apps: it shows the component tree with each component's props and state, and has a Profiler for measuring renders.
A chart that draws a program's nested work as stacked bars, each as wide as the time it took, so the slowest parts stand out.
Drawing only the rows of a long list that are currently visible on screen, and swapping them as the user scrolls, instead of creating thousands of elements.
A React component, <Suspense fallback={...}>, that shows its fallback (such as a spinner) while something inside it is still loading, then shows the real content.
Breaking an app's JavaScript into several smaller files so the browser downloads each part only when it is needed, instead of everything up front.
In React, a state update marked as not urgent with startTransition. React works on it in the background, can interrupt it for urgent updates like typing, and keeps showing the old screen meanwhile.
React's ability to prepare a new screen in the background, pause or abandon that work when something more urgent happens, and show it only when it is complete.
In React 19, an async function run as a transition, usually to save data: React tracks whether it is still running and applies its state updates when it finishes. Form action props take Actions.
Showing the expected result of an action straight away, such as a sent message appearing at once, before the server confirms it, and undoing it if it fails.
A component that catches errors thrown while rendering the components inside it and shows a fallback message instead of letting the whole app disappear.
A React component written as a JavaScript class with a render method instead of as a function. It is the older style; today it is only needed for error boundaries.
React's internal record for one component or element on the page: its type, props, state and links to its child, sibling and parent. Rendering works through fibers one at a time.
React's internal priority label for an update, such as urgent for typing or low for a transition, used to decide which updates to work on first.
A glitch where different parts of the same screen show different versions of some data, because the data changed while React was part-way through rendering.
Data kept outside React, such as a state library's store or a browser value like the online status, which components read and subscribe to for changes.
React components that run only on the server or when the app is built. They can read data directly, and their code is never sent to the browser.
In an app that uses Server Components, the components that are also sent to the browser so they can use state, Effects and event handlers. A file starting with "use client" holds them.
The compact description of Server Components' output that the server sends to the browser, which React uses to update the page.
An async function marked "use server" that runs on the server but can be called from browser code; calling it sends a request to the server behind the scenes.
Building a page so its basics, such as submitting a form, work with plain HTML, and JavaScript then makes it nicer when it loads.
The step where React in the browser takes over HTML that was produced on the server, attaching event handlers and state so the page becomes interactive.
An error where the browser's first render produces different output from the HTML the server sent, so React can't simply take it over.
React hydrating each Suspense section of a server-rendered page separately, and doing first the section the user is trying to interact with.
In server rendering, the outer part of a page (layout, headings and loading placeholders) that can be sent to the browser right away, before slower parts are ready.
Waiting until something has stopped changing for a short moment before reacting, such as searching only once the user pauses typing.
A small storage area the browser keeps for each website, holding text under names you choose. It survives reloading the page and restarting the browser.
A chain of loading steps where each starts only after the previous one finished, so their waiting times add up.
An automated test that drives a real browser through a whole task the way a user would, such as signing up and logging in.

concepts.name: What React is
concepts.summary: React is a library for building the screens of web apps out of components: small functions that describe what to show for the current data.
concepts.why: React's core idea, that the screen is worked out from your data, makes every later feature feel like a consequence rather than a rule to memorise.
concepts.body:
In the JavaScript lessons you changed a page by hand: find an element with `querySelector`, then set its text. In a big app, such as a chat or a shop, that means hundreds of such steps, and the page easily stops matching your data.

**React** is a **library**, a collection of ready-made code you call from your own program, for building **user interfaces** (UI): the screens, buttons, forms and text people see and use.

With React you don't change the page step by step. You write **components**: functions that take some data and return a description of what their part of the screen should look like.

When the data changes, React calls your components again to get the new description. This is called **rendering**. React then compares the new description with the old one and changes only the parts of the page that differ. You never touch the DOM yourself.

This is the central idea: **UI = f(state)**. Here *state* means the data your app is holding right now, such as the messages in a chat, and *f* is your component. You describe what the screen should look like for the current state, not how to get there from the previous screen.

That style is called **declarative**: like handing someone a shopping list rather than step-by-step directions round the shop. The step-by-step style you used with the DOM is called **imperative**.

A few more things worth knowing up front:

- React focuses on drawing the screen and keeping it in step with data. Other jobs, such as showing a different screen for each web address, come from other libraries or from a **framework**: a bigger toolkit built on React that sets the structure of your app for you. Next.js and React Router are popular ones.
- Modern components are plain functions. Older code wrote them as classes; you won't need that style for new code.

React 19, the current version, adds powerful features for forms, for running components on the server, and for making apps faster automatically. This course climbs from your first component to those features and on to how React works inside.
takeaways: React components are functions that describe what the screen should show for the current data
When data changes, React re-renders and updates the page for you (declarative, not imperative)
React draws the UI; other libraries or a framework add things like moving between pages
pitfalls: Expecting React alone to do everything an app needs: moving between pages and loading data usually come from other libraries or a framework.

quiz.q: What does 'declarative' mean in the context of React?
options: You describe the UI for the current state and React updates the page to match
You call DOM methods in the right order to update the page
You declare all variables with const
You write HTML templates in separate files
quiz.explain: Components describe the screen you want for the current data; React works out which page changes are needed to get there.

concepts.name: Creating a project with Vite
concepts.summary: Create a React project with Vite, learn what each file does, and run the app on your own computer while you edit it.
concepts.why: Every React project needs a few tools to run; Vite is the standard lightweight choice when you aren't using a framework.
concepts.body:
Browsers can't run React code as you write it. It uses **JSX**, HTML-like tags inside JavaScript (the next lessons cover it), and a real app is spread over many files. So a **build tool** first translates your code into plain JavaScript and bundles the files together. For React, the usual choice is **Vite**. You install Vite and React with **npm**, the **package manager** that comes with Node.js. A **package** is code someone has published under a name, like `react` or `vite`; npm downloads packages into your project's `node_modules` folder. In a terminal, run: ```bash npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react cd my-app npm install npm run dev ``` The first line creates a project folder from Vite's ready-made React starter. `npm install` downloads the packages it needs. `npm run dev` starts a **dev server**: a small server on your own computer that sends your app to your browser. Open the address it prints (usually `http://localhost:5173`). Leave it running while you work. Save a file and the page updates at once; **Fast Refresh** even keeps what was on screen, such as text you typed. Using `--template react-ts` instead picks **TypeScript**: JavaScript plus type labels such as `name: string`, which a checker reads to catch mistakes before the code runs. These lessons use plain JavaScript. The important files: - `index.html` is the one real page. It holds an empty `
` and loads `src/main.jsx`, the **entry point**: the file where your code starts running. - `src/main.jsx` tells React to take over that empty div and draw your `App` component inside it, wrapped in ``, a development helper explained later. - `src/App.jsx` is your first component. Everything else is components imported from here. - `vite.config.js` holds Vite's settings, including the React add-on that translates JSX. - `package.json` lists your project's packages and the commands `npm run` knows. When the app is ready to publish, `npm run build` writes the finished files into a `dist/` folder: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript that any server can send to browsers. `npm run preview` lets you check that build first. The `import` lines at the top of each file are ordinary modules. A name without a path, as in `import { useState } from "react"`, means an installed package.
takeaways: `npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react` creates a project; `npm install` fetches its packages
`npm run dev` runs the app locally and updates it as you save; `npm run build` makes the files to publish
`createRoot(el).render(<App />)` in `src/main.jsx` is where React takes over the page
pitfalls: Starting new projects with Create React App, which is no longer maintained.

quiz.q: In a Vite React app, what does createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />) do?
options: Translates JSX into plain JavaScript
Starts the development server
Takes over the empty #root element and draws the App component inside it
Creates a new HTML file for the app
quiz.explain: createRoot connects React to an element already on the page; render puts your App component inside it.

concepts.name: Your first components
concepts.summary: Define components as capitalised functions that return JSX, nest them, and export them from modules.
concepts.why: Components are the building blocks of every React app; splitting a screen into small components is the main design skill.
concepts.body:
A **component** is a JavaScript function whose name starts with a capital letter and which returns JSX. You then use it like an HTML tag: ```jsx function Avatar() { return ; } ``` Writing `` anywhere now shows that image. Components can use other components, so an app forms a **component tree**, like a family tree: `App` contains `Header`, `Feed` and `Sidebar`; `Feed` contains many `Post`s, and so on. Components side by side under the same parent are called siblings. The rules: - **Capitalise names.** `` is treated as an HTML tag; `` calls your function. - **Return one outer element.** To return several elements side by side, wrap them in a `
`, or in a **Fragment**, written `<>...`, which groups them without adding anything to the page. - **Define components at the top level** of a file, never inside another component. One defined inside another is a brand-new function each time the outer one renders, so React treats it as a different component and throws away everything it held, such as text typed into it. - **Export them** to use them in other files: `export default function Profile()` or `export function Avatar()`. Keep components small and focused. A good rule of thumb: if a piece of the screen is reused, or a component's JSX no longer fits on your screen, pull part of it out into its own component. Where you draw these lines also matters later, when you decide which component holds which data.
takeaways: A component is a capitalised function that returns JSX
Use `<>...</>` (a Fragment) to return several elements without adding a wrapper to the page
Declare components at the top level of a file and import/export them like any module
pitfalls: Defining a component inside another component, which makes React throw away its contents on every render.

quiz.q: Why should you not declare function Item() inside the body of function List()?
options: It is a syntax error
Item can then only be used once
JSX cannot reference inner functions
Item is a brand-new function on every render, so React throws it away and rebuilds it each time
quiz.explain: React recognises a component by its function; a function created afresh on each render looks like a different component.

concepts.name: JSX
concepts.summary: Write markup in JavaScript with JSX: curly braces for expressions, camelCase attributes, className and style objects.
concepts.why: JSX is how every component describes its output; its few rules differ from HTML in ways that trip up beginners.
concepts.body:
**JSX** lets you write HTML-like tags inside JavaScript. Browsers don't understand it: the build tool (Vite) translates each tag into an ordinary function call, such as `jsx("h1", {...})`, which creates a plain object describing the element. So JSX is just JavaScript values: you can store it in variables, return it and pass it around. Curly braces switch back to JavaScript. Inside `{}` you can put any **expression**: a variable, `user.name`, `formatDate(d)`, a ternary. Statements like `if` or `for` don't fit inside braces; compute values before the `return` instead. How JSX differs from HTML: - Every tag must be closed: ``, `
`. - Attributes are camelCase JavaScript property names: `className` (not `class`), `htmlFor`, `onClick`, `tabIndex`. `aria-*` (labels for screen readers) and `data-*` attributes keep their dashes. - `style` takes an object: `style={{ color: "red", fontSize: 14 }}`. The outer braces mean "JavaScript", the inner ones are the object. - Text in braces is always shown as plain text, never read as HTML, so `{userInput}` can't sneak code into your page (the XSS attack from the DOM lesson). What shows up: strings and numbers appear as text; `null`, `undefined`, `true` and `false` render nothing; arrays render each item. Objects are not valid children, so `{user}` throws; render `{user.name}`. Comments inside JSX go in braces: `{/* note */}`.
takeaways: `{}` embeds any JavaScript expression; compute statements before `return`
Use `className`, `htmlFor` and camelCase event/attribute names; close every tag
`style={{ ... }}` takes an object; text in braces is never read as HTML
pitfalls: Rendering an object directly (`{user}`) instead of one of its properties; React throws 'Objects are not valid as a React child'.

quiz.q: Which JSX is valid?
options: {if (ok) 'yes'}
{ok ? 'yes' : 'no'}
yes
quiz.explain: Braces take expressions (a ternary works, if doesn't), style needs an object, and every tag must be closed.

concepts.name: Props
concepts.summary: Pass data to components through props, destructure them, set defaults, and pass JSX as children.
concepts.why: Props are how components are configured and composed; nearly every component you write takes some.
concepts.body:
**Props** (short for properties) are the inputs to a component. You pass them like HTML attributes, and React collects them into one object that is the function's first argument:

```jsx
<Avatar person={{ name: "Lin" }} size={100} />

function Avatar({ person, size = 48 }) { ... }
```

Destructuring in the parameter list is the usual style, and a default value (`size = 48`) applies when the prop is missing or `undefined`. Any JavaScript value can be a prop: strings, numbers, objects, arrays, functions and JSX.

The special **`children`** prop holds whatever you nest between a component's tags. It is how you build wrappers like cards, layouts and dialogs that don't need to know what's inside them:

```jsx
<Card><Avatar person={p} /></Card>   // Card receives children
```

You can forward a bag of props with spread, `<Avatar {...props} />`, which is handy in small wrapper components; use it sparingly, as it hides what is being passed.

Props are **read-only**. A component must never modify its props; they belong to the parent. When something needs to change over time, that's **state**, which you'll meet shortly. When the parent re-renders with new props, the child simply renders again with the new values.

In TypeScript, you describe props with a type: `function Avatar({ size }: { size: number })`, or a named `type AvatarProps = {...}`.
takeaways: Props arrive as one object; destructure them and give defaults in the parameter list
`children` is whatever is nested between the tags, enabling wrapper components
Props are read-only; values that change over time belong in state
pitfalls: Mutating a prop (e.g. `props.items.push(x)`): the parent owns that data and won't know it changed.

quiz.q: Given function Badge({ label = 'New' }), what label does <Badge label={undefined} /> show?
options: Nothing
'undefined'
'New'
It throws an error
quiz.explain: Destructuring defaults apply when the value is undefined, whether the prop is missing or passed as undefined.

quiz.q: What does a Layout component receive in children for <Layout><Nav /><Main /></Layout>?
options: The two elements <Nav /> and <Main />
Nothing; children must be passed explicitly as a prop
Only the first element
The rendered DOM nodes
quiz.explain: Nested JSX is passed in the children prop; here it is the two elements.

concepts.name: Conditional rendering
concepts.summary: Show different UI depending on conditions with if/return, the ternary operator and &&.
concepts.why: Almost every component has states like loading, empty or error that render differently.
concepts.body:
Because JSX is JavaScript, conditional UI uses ordinary JavaScript. There are three common ways to do it.

**Early return with `if`** when a whole branch differs:

```jsx
if (!user) return <LoginPrompt />;
return <Dashboard user={user} />;
```

Returning `null` renders nothing, which is how a component hides itself.

**The ternary** `cond ? a : b` inside JSX for small either/or choices: `{isPacked ? <s>{name}</s> : name}`.

**Logical AND** `cond && <Thing />` when there is no else branch. If the condition is false, React renders nothing.

The classic gotcha with `&&`: if the left side is the number `0`, the expression evaluates to `0`, and React shows the number 0 on the page. `{messages.length && <Badge />}` shows "0" when the list is empty. Make the left side a real boolean: `{messages.length > 0 && <Badge />}`.

You can also put JSX in a variable and assign it conditionally before the `return`, which keeps complicated logic out of the markup:

```jsx
let content = <Spinner />;
if (error) content = <ErrorMessage error={error} />;
else if (data) content = <Results data={data} />;
```

When the nested ternaries start to pile up, that variable pattern, or extracting a small component, is the readable fix.
takeaways: Use `if` with early return for whole branches; return `null` to render nothing
Use `cond ? a : b` for either/or and `cond && x` for show/hide
Keep the left side of `&&` boolean: `count > 0 && ...`, not `count && ...`
pitfalls: `{items.length && <List />}` renders a stray 0 when the array is empty.

quiz.q:
What does {count &&

Items

} render when count is 0?
options: Nothing
The text 0
Items
false
quiz.explain: 0 && x evaluates to 0, and numbers are rendered as text; false, null and undefined render nothing.

concepts.name: Rendering lists and keys
concepts.summary: Turn arrays into elements with map and filter, and give each item a stable key so React can track it.
concepts.why: Lists are everywhere, and wrong keys cause subtle bugs where typed text or other details stick to the wrong item.
concepts.body:
To render a list, transform your data array into an array of JSX elements, usually with `map`, and filter first with `filter` if needed: ```jsx const items = people .filter(p => p.active) .map(p =>
  • {p.name}
    • ); return
      {items}
    ; ``` Every element in an array needs a **`key`** prop: a string or number that uniquely identifies that item among its siblings. Keys tell React which item is which between renders. When you insert, delete or reorder items, React uses keys to keep each item's page elements, and anything the user typed into them, attached to the right item, instead of rebuilding everything or, worse, mixing items up. Good keys come from the data itself: the id each item already has (for example, the number a server gave it), or an id you create once when the item is made, with `crypto.randomUUID()`, which returns a random unique string. Rules: - Keys must be unique among siblings, not globally. - Keys must be **stable**: the same item gets the same key on every render. - Don't use the array index if the list can be reordered, filtered or have items inserted; the index then refers to a different item and anything tied to the row (like typed-in text) follows the position, not the item. Index is acceptable only for static lists. - Never generate keys during render (`key={Math.random()}`); every render then creates brand-new components. The key goes on the outermost element returned from `map`. If you need to return several elements per item, use `` (import `Fragment` from `react`), since the short `<>` form can't take a key. Keys are not passed to your component as a prop; pass the id separately if the child needs it.
takeaways: Render arrays with `map` (and `filter`); each element needs a `key`
Keys must be unique among siblings and stable across renders, ideally ids from the data
Avoid index keys for lists that change order or contents; never use random keys
pitfalls: Using the array index as key in an editable or sortable list, so typed text ends up on the wrong row.

quiz.q: A todo list uses key={index}. You delete the first todo; each row has a text box the user has typed into. What happens?
options: Everything works correctly
React throws a duplicate key error
All inputs are cleared
The typed text stays in place by position, so it now appears next to the wrong todo
quiz.explain: With index keys, item 2 now has key 0, so React reuses the first row's elements, typed text included, for it.

concepts.name: Responding to events
concepts.summary: Attach event handlers with onClick and friends, pass handlers as props, and use the event object.
concepts.why: Events are how users interact with your UI and the trigger for nearly every state change.
concepts.body:
You handle events by passing a **function** to a prop written in camelCase (words joined, later ones capitalised) such as `onClick`, `onChange`, `onSubmit` or `onKeyDown`:

```jsx
<button onClick={handleClick}>Save</button>
```

Pass the function, don't call it. `onClick={handleClick()}` runs during render and passes its return value. When you need arguments, wrap it: `onClick={() => deleteItem(id)}`.

Handlers receive an event object much like the one from `addEventListener`. React wraps the browser's own event so it behaves the same in every browser, with the familiar parts: `e.target`, `e.preventDefault()`, `e.stopPropagation()`, `e.key`. Events bubble up through the component tree just like in the DOM, so a click on a button also reaches an `onClick` on its parent unless you stop it. (Behind the scenes React uses event delegation: one listener at the top of your app, not one per element.)

Very often you pass handlers **as props**. The parent decides what happens; the child decides when:

```jsx
function Toolbar({ onPlay }) {
  return <button onClick={onPlay}>Play</button>;
}
```

By convention, props that take handlers are named `onSomething` and the functions that implement them `handleSomething`.

For forms, call `e.preventDefault()` in an `onSubmit` handler to stop the browser's full-page submit, or use React 19's `action` prop, covered later. Handlers are where side effects belong: they may update state, send data to a server or record what users click, because they run in response to a user action rather than during rendering.
takeaways: Pass a function to `onClick`, don't call it: `onClick={fn}` or `onClick={() => fn(id)}`
Events bubble through the component tree; `e.stopPropagation()` and `e.preventDefault()` work as in the DOM
Name handler props `onX` and implementations `handleX`; side effects belong in handlers
pitfalls: Writing `onClick={remove(id)}`, which calls `remove` on every render instead of on click.

quiz.q: What is wrong with <button onClick={setOpen(true)}>Open</button>?
options: setOpen(true) runs during rendering instead of on click, which causes an infinite re-render loop
Nothing
Event handlers cannot call state setters
onClick must be lowercase
quiz.explain: The expression is evaluated during render; use onClick={() => setOpen(true)} to defer it to the click.

concepts.name: State with useState
concepts.summary: Let a component remember values between renders with useState, see why state is a snapshot, and use updater functions.
concepts.why: State is what makes a UI interactive; misunderstanding when it updates is the most common React bug.
concepts.body:
Regular variables don't survive re-renders, and changing them doesn't tell React to update the page. For data that changes over time and should change the screen, use **state**: values React keeps for a component between renders.

```jsx
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
```

`useState` returns the current value and a setter: a function that changes it. Calling the setter stores the new value and **schedules a re-render**; on that render `useState` returns the new value. Each place you use a component gets its own state: render `<Counter />` twice and you get two independent counts.

`useState` is a **Hook**: one of React's special functions whose names start with `use`. Hooks must be called at the top level of a component (not inside conditions, loops or nested functions), because React matches them up by call order.

The key mental model: **state is a snapshot**, a frozen copy of the value as it was when this render started. During one render, `count` is a constant. Setting it doesn't change the variable you already have, it requests a new render:

```jsx
setCount(count + 1);
setCount(count + 1);   // still count + 1: both read the same snapshot
console.log(count);    // old value
```

React also groups all updates from one event into a single re-render (this is called **batching**). When the next value depends on the previous one, pass an **updater function** instead: a function that receives the latest value, including updates still waiting, and returns the next one:

```jsx
setCount(c => c + 1);
setCount(c => c + 1);  // +2
```

If initial state is expensive to compute, pass a function: `useState(() => buildIndex(data))` runs only on the first render.

Only store what can't be computed. If a value can be derived from props or other state (a full name from first and last, a filtered list), compute it during render instead of storing a copy in state and keeping it up to date.
takeaways: `const [v, setV] = useState(init)`; calling the setter schedules a re-render
State is a snapshot: the variable doesn't change until the next render
Use `setV(prev => next)` when the new value depends on the old one
Call Hooks only at the top level; derive values instead of duplicating them in state
pitfalls: Reading state right after setting it and expecting the new value.
Copying props into state and then wondering why it doesn't update when the prop changes.

quiz.q: count is 0. A click handler runs setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1); setCount(c => c + 1). What is count after the re-render?
quiz.explain: The first two both set 0 + 1 = 1 from the snapshot; the updater then adds 1 to the queued value, giving 2.

quiz.q: Why must Hooks not be called inside an if statement?
options: It is slower
Hooks can only be called in event handlers
TypeScript cannot type them
React identifies each Hook by its call order, which must be the same on every render
quiz.explain: State is stored in a list per component and matched by position, so the order of Hook calls must never change.

concepts.name: Updating objects and arrays
concepts.summary: Treat objects and arrays in state as immutable: copy them with spread, map and filter instead of mutating.
concepts.why: Mutating state is the classic cause of 'my UI doesn't update'; immutable updates are the fix and a core React habit.
concepts.body:
State can hold objects and arrays, but you must treat them as **immutable**. React decides whether to re-render by checking whether the new value is the very same object as the old one (with `Object.is`). If you mutate the existing object and pass it back, React sees no change. Even if something else causes a render, you've also altered the snapshot an earlier render was using.

So instead of changing data, **create a new copy** with the change applied.

Objects: spread the old properties, then list the ones to change.

```jsx
setPerson({ ...person, email: newEmail });
setPerson({ ...person, address: { ...person.address, city } }); // nested: copy each level
```

Arrays: use methods that return a new array.

- Add: `[...items, item]` or `[item, ...items]`
- Remove: `items.filter(i => i.id !== id)`
- Replace or update one: `items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, done: true } : i)`
- Insert: `[...items.slice(0, n), item, ...items.slice(n)]`
- Sort/reverse: copy first, `[...items].sort(cmp)`, or use the newer `toSorted()` / `toReversed()`, which return sorted copies

Avoid `push`, `splice`, `sort`, `reverse` and direct assignment (`items[0] = x`, `person.name = x`) on state.

If deeply nested updates get painful, that's often a sign the state should have a flatter, simpler shape (store items by id, keep `selectedId` rather than a copy of the selected object). The **Immer** library (`useImmer`) lets you write mutating-looking code that produces immutable copies, which some teams prefer for complex structures.
takeaways: Never mutate state; build a new object or array and pass it to the setter
Objects: `{ ...obj, key: v }`; nested objects need a copy at each level
Arrays: add with spread, remove with `filter`, update with `map`, sort a copy
pitfalls: `items.push(x); setItems(items)` passes the same array reference, so React may skip the update.

quiz.q: Which update correctly marks the todo with id 7 as done?
options: todos.find(t => t.id === 7).done = true; setTodos(todos)
setTodos(todos.map(t => t.id === 7 ? { ...t, done: true } : t))
setTodos(todos.map(t => { if (t.id === 7) t.done = true; return t; }))
todos[6].done = true; setTodos([...todos])
quiz.explain: Only the map with a spread copy creates a new object for the changed item; the others mutate existing state objects.

concepts.name: Forms and controlled inputs
concepts.summary: Build forms with controlled inputs bound to state, or uncontrolled inputs read on submit with FormData.
concepts.why: Forms are how users type information into an app, and the controlled/uncontrolled choice shapes how you handle it.
takeaways: Controlled: `value` + `onChange` bound to state; React state is the source of truth
Uncontrolled: `defaultValue` and read values on submit with `new FormData(form)`
Call `e.preventDefault()` in `onSubmit` (or use the React 19 `action` prop)
pitfalls: Initialising controlled-input state to `undefined`, which flips the input from uncontrolled to controlled.

quiz.q: An <input value={text} /> has no onChange handler. What happens when the user types?
options: The text updates normally
React throws an error and removes the form
The input does not change, because its value is always forced to the state value
The input becomes uncontrolled automatically
quiz.explain: A controlled input shows exactly the value prop; without an onChange that updates state, typing has no effect (and React warns).

concepts.name: Thinking in React and lifting state
concepts.summary: Break a UI into components, find the minimal state, decide which component owns it, and lift state up to share it.
concepts.why: Deciding where state lives is the core design decision in every React app; get it right and the rest follows.
concepts.body:
The React docs describe a design method that scales from a widget to an app:

- **Break the UI into a component tree.** Draw boxes around parts of a sketch of the screen (a mockup); each box with one responsibility is a component.
- **Build a static version** that renders from props, with no state.
- **Find the minimal state.** Ask of each piece of data: is it passed in from a parent? Does it stay the same over time? Can it be computed from other state or props? If any answer is yes, it's not state. In a filterable product table, the product list (a prop) and the filtered list (derived) aren't state; the search text and the "in stock only" checkbox are.
- **Decide who owns each piece of state**: the closest common parent of all components that use it.
- **Let children report changes**: children change the owner's state by calling functions passed down to them as props.

When two siblings need the same data, use **lifting state up**: remove the state from the children, put it in their parent, and pass the value and a function to change it down to them. The children are then driven entirely by props, which makes them easy to coordinate (say, an accordion, a stack of collapsible panels where only one is open at a time).

Data flows **down** through props and events flow **up** through callbacks. That one-way flow is why React apps stay easy to reason about: for any value on screen, there's exactly one component that owns it.

Avoid duplicating state (storing `selectedItem` as a copy when `selectedId` would do) and avoid contradictory state (`isSending` and `isSent` both true). If state lives too high, many components re-render needlessly and props get passed through many layers; later lessons show tools for that.
takeaways: State is data that changes, isn't passed in, and can't be computed from anything else
Put state in the closest common parent of the components that use it
Data flows down as props; changes flow up through callback props
pitfalls: Keeping the same data in two components' state and trying to keep the copies matching instead of lifting it up.

quiz.q: A SearchBar and a ProductTable (siblings) both need the search text. Where should that state live?
options: In their closest common parent, passed down as props
In SearchBar, which then sends it to ProductTable directly
In both components, each keeping its own copy
In a global variable
quiz.explain: Lift shared state to the nearest common parent; it passes the value to both and a setter callback to SearchBar.

quiz.q: Which of these should NOT be state in a filterable list?
options: The text in the search box
The list of items filtered by the search text
Whether the 'show archived' checkbox is ticked
Which item the user has selected
quiz.explain: The filtered list can be computed during render from the items and the search text, so it shouldn't be stored.

concepts.name: Pure components and Strict Mode
concepts.summary: Keep rendering pure (same inputs, same JSX, no side effects) and use Strict Mode to catch impure components during development.
concepts.why: React relies on purity to re-render, pause and reuse work safely; impure components break in subtle, intermittent ways.
concepts.body:
React assumes every component behaves like a **pure function** while rendering: a function whose result depends only on its inputs and which changes nothing outside itself.

- **Same inputs, same output.** Given the same props and state, it returns the same JSX.
- **No side effects while rendering.** It doesn't change variables or objects that existed before the render, doesn't touch the DOM, doesn't start requests or timers, doesn't save anything to the browser's storage.

Creating and mutating *local* variables is fine; it's changing pre-existing things that's forbidden. A counter defined outside the component and incremented during render, for example, gives different results each time the component renders.

Why this matters: React may call your component more often than you expect, start a render and throw the result away when something more urgent comes in, render parts of the tree in a different order, or skip rendering and reuse an earlier result. Later lessons cover these features; pure components make all of them safe.

Side effects still have a home:

- **Event handlers** for effects caused by a user action (click, submit, type).
- **Effects** (`useEffect`, next lesson) for keeping a component in step with something outside React, such as a chat connection, for as long as it's on screen.

**Strict Mode** (`<StrictMode>` wrapping your app, as in Vite's starter files) helps find impure components, in development only. It renders each component twice, and runs some setup code twice when a component first appears, as later lessons explain. Pure code behaves the same; impure code shows doubled output or broken behaviour, pointing you at the bug. That's why you may see `console.log` output twice while developing. The finished build you publish, the **production** build, doesn't double anything.
takeaways: Rendering must be pure: same inputs, same JSX, no changes to pre-existing values
Put side effects in event handlers, or in Effects when they keep something outside React in step
Strict Mode renders twice in development to expose impure code
pitfalls: Removing `<StrictMode>` to 'fix' doubled console output or a double request instead of fixing the impure code.

quiz.q: Under Strict Mode in development, a component logs once per render. You see two logs when it first appears. Why?
options: The component has a bug that renders it twice in production too
React always renders every component twice
The log is duplicated by the browser console
Strict Mode intentionally renders components twice in development to detect impure rendering
quiz.explain: Strict Mode double-invokes rendering in development only; pure components are unaffected by it.

concepts.name: useEffect and synchronizing
concepts.summary: Use Effects to keep a component in step with systems outside React, with the right dependency array and cleanup, and know when not to use one.
concepts.why: Effects are the most misused Hook; knowing what they're for prevents bugs, wasted re-renders and out-of-order data.
takeaways: Effects keep outside systems in step with a component and run after React updates the page
List every value the Effect reads in its dependency array; return a cleanup that undoes setup
Derived data belongs in render and user-triggered work in event handlers, not in Effects
pitfalls: Leaving values out of the dependency array to stop an Effect re-running, so it keeps reading out-of-date values.
Chains of Effects that set state to trigger other Effects, instead of computing values during render.

quiz.q: store.subscribe(cb) returns an unsubscribe function. Does useEffect(() => store.subscribe(cb), [cb]) clean up correctly?
options: Yes: the arrow function returns the unsubscribe function, which React uses as the cleanup
No: the cleanup must be written as return () => { ... } in a block body
No: subscriptions can only be cleaned up when the dependency array is empty
No: cleanup only runs in production builds
quiz.explain: The concise arrow body returns subscribe's return value (an unsubscribe function), which React uses as the cleanup.

quiz.q: A component stores fullName in state and updates it in an effect whenever firstName or lastName changes. What's the better approach?
options: Add fullName to the effect's dependencies
Give the effect an empty dependency array []
Compute const fullName = firstName + ' ' + lastName during render
Move the effect to the parent component
quiz.explain: Derived values should be calculated during rendering; the effect causes an extra render with a stale value.

concepts.name: Refs, DOM access and portals
concepts.summary: Keep values that don't affect the screen with useRef, reach page elements through ref, and draw content elsewhere on the page with createPortal.
concepts.why: Focusing inputs, measuring elements, holding timer ids and integrating non-React code all need refs.
takeaways: `useRef` holds a mutable `.current` that keeps its value across renders without triggering them
Pass a ref to `ref={...}` to get the DOM node; in React 19 `ref` is a normal prop for components
Don't read/write refs during render; use `createPortal` to render into another DOM node
pitfalls: Storing something in a ref that the screen displays, so the screen doesn't update when it changes.

quiz.q: You store a click count in a ref and render {countRef.current}. Clicking increments countRef.current. What does the user see?
options: The count updating on every click
The count updating once per second
An error, because refs can't be rendered
The old value, until something else causes a re-render
quiz.explain: Changing ref.current doesn't trigger a render; values that are displayed belong in state.

quiz.q: What stays the same for content rendered with createPortal into document.body?
options: Its position in the DOM tree
Its position in the React tree, so events bubble to the React parent
Its CSS inheritance from the parent element
Nothing; it becomes a separate app
quiz.explain: Portals change only where the DOM nodes go; React-wise the children remain under their parent.

concepts.name: Custom Hooks
concepts.summary: Move reusable logic that uses state and Effects into your own use-prefixed functions.
concepts.why: Custom Hooks are React's main tool for reusing behaviour and keeping components readable.
takeaways: A custom Hook is a `use`-prefixed function that calls other Hooks
It shares logic, not state: every call has its own state
Name Hooks by purpose (`useOnlineStatus`), not by lifecycle (`useMount`)
pitfalls: Prefixing a plain helper with `use` even though it calls no Hooks, which needlessly restricts where it can be called.

quiz.q: Two components both call useCounter(). One increments its count. What happens to the other's count?
options: It increments too, because they share the Hook
It resets to the initial value
Nothing; each call has its own independent state
React throws because a Hook was used twice
quiz.explain: Custom Hooks reuse stateful logic, but each call creates separate state for the calling component.

concepts.name: Context
concepts.summary: Pass data deeply without prop drilling using createContext, a provider, and useContext or use.
concepts.why: Themes, the current user, locale and similar app-wide values need to reach distant components cleanly.
concepts.body:
Passing props through many layers that don't use them (**prop drilling**) gets tedious. **Context** lets a parent make a value available to every component below it, however deep.

Three steps:

```jsx
const ThemeContext = createContext("light");          // 1. create, with a default
<ThemeContext value="dark"><Page /></ThemeContext>     // 2. provide
const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);                // 3. read
```

In React 19 you render the context itself as the **provider**, the component that supplies the value (`<ThemeContext value=...>`); `<ThemeContext.Provider>` still works but is on its way out. A component reads the value from the **nearest** provider above it; with none, it gets the default from `createContext`. Providers can be nested to give a different value to one part of the tree.

React 19's `use(ThemeContext)` reads context too, and unlike `useContext` it can be called inside conditions and loops.

When the provided value changes, every component reading that context re-renders. Two consequences:

- If you provide an object, `value={{ user, setUser }}` creates a new object each render, re-rendering all consumers. Keep it the same object between renders (the Memoization lesson shows how), or split it into separate contexts for rarely and frequently changing parts.
- For large, fast-changing data that many components share, a dedicated state library (such as Zustand or Redux) that re-renders only the components needing each piece can fit better.

A common pairing is context **plus a reducer** (`useReducer`, the Reducers lesson): a top-level component holds the state and shares it, with the function that changes it, through context, wrapped in your own Hook function like `useTasks()`.

Before reaching for context, try composition: passing JSX as `children` often removes the drilling with no new concepts.
takeaways: `createContext(default)`, provide with `<Ctx value={...}>`, read with `useContext(Ctx)` or `use(Ctx)`
Consumers read the nearest provider above them and re-render when its value changes
Keep provided objects stable and split contexts by update frequency
pitfalls: Calling `useContext` in the same component that renders the provider: it reads the provider above, not its own.

quiz.q: A component calls useContext(ThemeContext) but no ThemeContext provider exists above it. What does it get?
options: The default value passed to createContext
undefined, always
An error is thrown
The value from the most recently rendered provider anywhere
quiz.explain: Without a provider in the ancestors, the context's default value is used.

concepts.name: Reducers with useReducer
concepts.summary: Consolidate complex state updates into a reducer function that handles dispatched actions.
concepts.why: When many event handlers update related state, a reducer makes the logic testable and easier to follow.
takeaways: `const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initial)`; handlers dispatch actions
Reducers are pure: `(state, action) => newState`, never mutating
Prefer a reducer when related state changes together or logic needs testing
pitfalls: Doing side effects (fetching, saving) inside the reducer instead of in the event handler.

quiz.q: Where should the request that saves the cart to the server go when using useReducer?
options: Inside the reducer's case for 'saved'
In the event handler, with dispatch used to record the result
In the initial state
In the default case of the switch
quiz.explain: Reducers must be pure; side effects belong in handlers, which then dispatch actions describing what happened.

concepts.name: Data fetching patterns
concepts.summary: Fetch data in Effects without out-of-order bugs, and know when a data library, a framework or use() is the better choice.
concepts.why: Every real app loads data; naive fetching shows the wrong data, loads slowly and repeats the same loading code everywhere.
takeaways: Fetch in an Effect keyed by its inputs, with an ignore flag or AbortController so old responses can't win
Real apps use a data library (TanStack Query, SWR) or a framework for caching and to avoid waterfalls
With React 19, `use(promise)` + Suspense reads cached or passed-in promises during render
pitfalls: Forgetting cleanup, so a slow earlier response overwrites the data for the current id.
Creating a new promise during render and passing it to `use()`, so the component never stops loading.

quiz.q: A profile page fetches in useEffect keyed by userId with no cleanup. The user clicks A then quickly B; A's response arrives last. What's shown?
options: B's profile
A loading spinner forever
An error
A's profile, even though B is selected
quiz.explain: Without an ignore flag or abort, A's late response calls setState after B's and overwrites it.

concepts.name: Styling approaches
concepts.summary: Choose between plain CSS, CSS Modules, utility CSS like Tailwind and CSS-in-JS, and use className and style correctly.
concepts.why: Every project picks a styling strategy early; knowing the trade-offs avoids painful migrations.
concepts.body:
React doesn't prescribe styling; it just gives you `className` and `style`. The main approaches:

- **Plain CSS files** imported into a module (`import "./App.css"`). Vite bundles them. Simple, but every class name applies across the whole app, so two files using `.title` clash more often as the app grows.
- **CSS Modules**: name the file `Button.module.css`, then `import styles from "./Button.module.css"` and use `className={styles.primary}`. Vite renames the classes so they only apply where that file is imported. It costs nothing extra in the browser and works in Vite and all frameworks out of the box.
- **Utility-first CSS** such as **Tailwind**: compose small classes in JSX (`className="px-4 py-2 rounded bg-blue-600"`). Very popular with React because styles live next to the JSX and the build removes classes you don't use.
- **CSS-in-JS** (styled-components, Emotion) defines styles in JavaScript. Libraries that build the styles in the browser while the app runs cost extra work and don't suit React's server features; others (vanilla-extract, Panda, StyleX) turn the styles into plain CSS files when you build.

Whatever you choose, conditional classes are just strings. Build them with a template literal or a helper like `clsx`: `className={clsx("tab", isActive && "tab-active")}`.

The `style` prop takes an object with camelCase properties and is best for truly dynamic values (a computed width, or a CSS variable: a named value like `--progress` that your CSS can use): `style={{ "--progress": pct + "%" }}`. Prefer classes for everything static.

React 19 also lets any component render `<title>`, `<meta>` and CSS `<link>` tags (with a `precedence` attribute). React moves them into the page's `<head>`, the part of the HTML that holds the title and settings, includes each CSS file only once, and waits for it to load before showing the content that needs it.
takeaways: `className` takes a string; build conditional classes with `clsx` or a helper
CSS Modules scope class names per file; Tailwind keeps utility classes in JSX
Use `style` for dynamic values; React 19 moves `<title>`, `<meta>` and CSS links into `<head>`
pitfalls: Picking a CSS-in-JS library that builds styles in the browser for an app using Server Components, where it needs awkward workarounds.

quiz.q: What does importing styles from './Card.module.css' give you that importing './Card.css' does not?
options: Class names that only apply where the file is imported, so they can't clash with others
Faster CSS parsing in the browser
Inline styles on every element
Automatic dark mode
quiz.explain: CSS Modules rewrite class names to unique ones and expose them as an object, so they can't clash.

concepts.name: Routing with React Router
concepts.summary: Show a different screen for each URL with React Router: routes, shared layouts, links, URL parameters and navigation.
concepts.why: Any app with several screens needs URLs that match what's showing; React itself doesn't include a router.
concepts.body:
React has no built-in **router**: the part of an app that picks which screen to show for the current URL (this job is called **routing**). The most widely used is **React Router** (version 7, imported from `react-router`). It works as a plain library in a Vite app, or as a full framework that also loads data and builds pages on the server. The library style looks like this:

```jsx
<BrowserRouter>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Layout />}>
      <Route index element={<Home />} />
      <Route path="users/:userId" element={<User />} />
      <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
    </Route>
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>
```

Key ideas:

- **Routes match the URL** and render their `element`. Paths can contain **dynamic segments** (`:userId`), read with `useParams()`.
- **Nested routes** build layouts. A parent route renders shared UI (header, sidebar) and an `<Outlet />` where the matching child appears. `index` marks the child shown at the parent's own path.
- **Navigate without reloading** using `<Link to="/users/42">` or `<NavLink>` (which knows when it's active). Plain `<a href>` triggers a full page load.
- **Navigating from code** after something happens: `const navigate = useNavigate(); navigate("/done")`.
- **Query strings** via `useSearchParams()`, which is a good home for filter and sort state because it survives reloads and can be shared as a link.

React Router's data mode (`createBrowserRouter` with a `loader` and `action` per route) and its framework mode go further: each screen's data starts loading at the same time as its code, before rendering, instead of one after another. Next.js and TanStack Router are popular alternatives.

If you publish the app as plain files, set up the server to send `index.html` for any path it doesn't recognise. Otherwise someone opening `/users/42` directly gets a "not found" (404) error, because no such file exists.
takeaways: Routes map URL patterns to elements; `:param` segments are read with `useParams`
Nested routes plus `<Outlet />` give shared layouts
Use `<Link>`/`useNavigate` to change screens without reloading; keep shareable screen state in the URL
pitfalls: Using `<a href>` for internal links, which reloads the whole app and loses state.

quiz.q: In a nested route setup, where does the matching child route render?
options: Replacing the parent's element entirely
At the end of document.body
Wherever the parent renders <Outlet />
In a new browser tab
quiz.explain: The parent route's element renders shared layout and an <Outlet /> placeholder for the active child.

concepts.name: Testing components
concepts.summary: Test components the way people use them with Vitest and React Testing Library: render, find elements by role, interact, check the result.
concepts.why: Tests that check behaviour rather than inner details let you restructure code and upgrade React with confidence.
takeaways: Render, find elements by role/label, interact with user-event, check what the user sees
`getBy` throws, `queryBy` returns null, `findBy` waits for async UI
Fake the network (MSW), not your components' insides
pitfalls: Using `getBy...` right after triggering an async load; use `await findBy...` so the test waits.

quiz.q: Which lookup should you use to wait for a heading that appears after data loads?
options: screen.getByRole('heading')
screen.queryByRole('heading')
container.querySelector('h1')
await screen.findByRole('heading')
quiz.explain: findBy queries return a promise that retries until the element appears or a timeout passes.

concepts.name: Rendering and reconciliation
concepts.summary: Understand the trigger, render and commit steps, how React compares old and new trees by type and key, and when state is kept or reset.
concepts.why: Knowing exactly when components re-render and when state survives explains most performance issues and 'my state reset' bugs.
concepts.body:
Every screen update goes through three steps:

- **Trigger**: the initial `root.render()`, or a state update in some component.
- **Render**: React calls your components to compute the new JSX. When a component re-renders, by default **all its descendants re-render too**, whether or not their props changed.
- **Commit**: React applies the smallest set of DOM changes needed (the **commit phase**). If the output is the same, the page isn't touched at all; rendering is not the same as redrawing the screen.

Producing the new tree and comparing it with the previous one is **reconciliation**. Comparing two arbitrary trees perfectly would be far too slow for big pages, so React uses two shortcut rules:

- Elements of **different types** at the same position produce different subtrees. Switching `<div>` to `<section>`, or `<Counter>` to `<Timer>`, removes the old part of the tree from the page (it **unmounts**, losing its state and elements) and **mounts** (adds) a new one.
- Among children, **keys** identify which element is which across renders.

This defines when **state is preserved**: state belongs to a position in the tree, not to the component function. Same component type at the same position keeps its state, even if you pass different props. `{isAdmin ? <Profile user={a} /> : <Profile user={b} />}` keeps one `Profile`'s state for both users.

To **reset** state deliberately, change the key: `<Profile key={user.id} user={user} />` makes each user a different component instance. That's the idiomatic way to reset a form when the selected item changes, instead of an effect.

Corollaries: never define components inside other components (new type every render), and don't flip a subtree's wrapper element type unless you want a remount. Because re-rendering cascades, pushing state down to the component that needs it, or passing static JSX as `children`, keeps renders small even without the caching tools of the next lesson.
takeaways: Updates go trigger, render, commit; re-rendering a parent re-renders its children by default
Same type at the same position preserves state; a different type or key remounts
Change a component's `key` to reset its state on purpose
pitfalls: Wrapping content in a different element conditionally (`<div>` vs `<span>`) and unexpectedly losing child state.

quiz.q: {edit ? <Form initial={a} /> : <Form initial={b} />} - the user types into the form, then edit flips. What happens to the typed text?
options: It's cleared because the props changed
It's preserved because the same component type is at the same position
React throws a reconciliation error
It moves to a new DOM node
quiz.explain: React sees a Form at the same position both times and keeps its state; add distinct keys to reset it.

quiz.q: When a parent component re-renders, what happens to a child whose props did not change (no special optimisation)?
options: It is skipped automatically
It is unmounted and remounted
It re-renders too
Only its event handlers are recreated
quiz.explain: By default React re-renders the whole subtree; the tools in the next lesson are needed to skip unchanged children.

concepts.name: Memoization and the React Compiler
concepts.summary: Skip unnecessary work with memo, useMemo and useCallback, and let the React Compiler apply memoization automatically.
concepts.why: Memoization fixes real slowdowns, but misapplied it adds complexity; the React Compiler changes when you need it by hand.
concepts.body:
Because re-rendering cascades, you sometimes want to skip work. **Memoization** means remembering a result so you can reuse it instead of working it out again. React offers three tools:

- **`memo(Component)`** skips re-rendering a component when its props are **shallowly equal** to last time: each prop is the same value or the very same object (`Object.is`), without looking inside objects.
- **`useMemo(() => compute(a, b), [a, b])`** caches a computed value between renders until a value in its dependency array changes.
- **`useCallback(fn, [deps])`** caches a function identity; it's `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`.

They work together. `memo` is defeated if a parent passes a new object or arrow function each render, since `{}` !== `{}`. So you keep those props stable with `useMemo`/`useCallback`. The same applies to values in Effect dependency arrays and to context values.

Use them when you've measured a problem: an expensive calculation (filtering thousands of rows), a large subtree that re-renders on every keystroke, or a value that must be stable for an effect. Memoizing everything costs memory and readability, and one unstable prop silently breaks the chain.

Often a structural fix is better: move state down into the component that uses it, or lift expensive content up and pass it as `children` so it isn't re-created when the wrapper's state changes.

The **React Compiler** (stable since v1.0) is an add-on for your build tool (`babel-plugin-react-compiler`, switched on in Vite's React plugin or the Next.js settings) that analyses your components and Hooks and inserts fine-grained memoization automatically, including for JSX and callbacks, and even after early returns. With it, most manual `memo`/`useMemo`/`useCallback` becomes unnecessary. It relies on your code following the Rules of React (pure render, no mutation of props/state, Hooks at top level) and skips components it can't prove safe; the React Hooks linter flags those. Manual memoization remains for when you need precise control, such as keeping an Effect's dependencies stable.
takeaways: `memo` skips renders on shallow-equal props; `useMemo` caches values; `useCallback` caches functions
A single new object or function prop defeats `memo`; measure before memoizing
The React Compiler memoizes automatically for code that follows the Rules of React
pitfalls: Wrapping a component in `memo` but passing an inline object or arrow function, so it re-renders anyway.

quiz.q: A memo-wrapped Chart receives options={{ color: 'red' }} written inline in the parent. The parent re-renders. Does Chart re-render?
options: Yes, because a new options object is created each render and fails the shallow comparison
No, memo compares deeply
No, because the values are identical
Only if Chart has state
quiz.explain: memo compares props with Object.is; a fresh object literal is never identical to the previous one.

quiz.q: What does the React Compiler require of your code to optimise it safely?
options: That all components are class components
That components follow the Rules of React, such as pure rendering and no mutation of props or state
That every component is wrapped in memo
That you remove all useState calls
quiz.explain: The compiler's analysis assumes the Rules of React; it bails out on components that break them.

concepts.name: Profiling performance
concepts.summary: Find slow renders with the React DevTools Profiler, the Profiler component and browser performance tools, then fix the real cause.
concepts.why: Performance work without measurement wastes time; the profiler shows exactly which components render, why, and for how long.
concepts.body:
Measure before optimising, and measure a **production build** (`npm run build && npm run preview`): development mode is much slower because of extra checks and Strict Mode double rendering.

The **React DevTools** browser extension has a Profiler tab; a **profiler** is a tool that measures where time goes. It records interactions. Start recording, perform the slow action, stop, and inspect each commit:

- The **flame graph** draws the component tree as bars, each as wide as the time it took; grey ones didn't render.
- The **ranked** view sorts components by time spent in each one itself (not counting its children), pointing at the expensive component.
- Enable "Record why each component rendered" to see whether it was a state change, a parent render, changed props (and which), or a context change.
- "Highlight updates when components render" visually flashes re-rendering components while you use the app.

Typical findings and fixes:

- A keystroke re-renders the whole page because state lives too high: move it down, or pass static parts as `children`.
- A memoized child re-renders because of an unstable prop: stabilise it (or adopt the React Compiler, which DevTools marks with a "Memo" badge).
- A single slow component: memoize the calculation, for a long list use **list virtualization**, drawing only the rows currently visible (TanStack Virtual, react-window), or mark the update as less urgent with `useTransition`/`useDeferredValue` (covered soon).

The browser's own **Performance** panel complements this; since React 19.2 it shows extra React rows with which updates React was working on and how long components took. To collect timings from code, wrap part of the tree in the `<Profiler id onRender>` component, which calls your function after each render. It's switched off in normal production builds; React offers a special profiling build for measuring real users.

Also look beyond React: very large JavaScript files (split them with `lazy`, covered next), code that makes the browser recalculate the layout over and over, and chains of slow network requests are frequent culprits.
takeaways: Profile production builds; development mode is deliberately slower
DevTools Profiler shows what rendered, how long, and why
Fix causes: state placement, unstable props, list virtualization, transitions, splitting large code files
pitfalls: Optimising based on development-mode timings or `console.log` output instead of a profile.

quiz.q: The Profiler shows a large table re-rendering on every keystroke in an unrelated search box higher up the page. What's the most direct fix?
options: Use a class component for the table
Turn off Strict Mode
Wrap the table in a portal
Move the search state down into a component that doesn't contain the table, or memoize the table
quiz.explain: The table re-renders because it sits under the component whose state changes; isolating the state or memoizing stops the cascade.

concepts.name: Suspense, lazy and use()
concepts.summary: Show loading states with Suspense boundaries, load code only when needed with `lazy`, and read promises during render with use().
concepts.why: Suspense replaces scattered isLoading flags with loading screens you declare once, and is the base of how React 19 loads data and sends pages in pieces.
concepts.body:
**Suspense** lets a component "wait" for something before rendering, while you declare the loading UI once, higher up:

```jsx
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>
  <Comments />
</Suspense>
```

If anything inside **suspends**, meaning it tells React it isn't ready yet, React shows the nearest boundary's `fallback` until it's ready, then reveals the content. Things that suspend:

- **`lazy`** components: `const Editor = lazy(() => import("./Editor.jsx"))` downloads that component's code only the first time it renders. This is **code splitting**: instead of one huge JavaScript file, users download each screen or feature when they need it.
- **`use(promise)`** in React 19: reads the value of a promise during render. If it's pending, the component suspends; if it rejects, the error goes to the nearest error boundary (a component that catches errors, covered soon).
- Suspense-enabled data sources: framework data loading, Server Components, TanStack Query's `useSuspenseQuery`.

`use` is special among Hooks: it can be called conditionally and in loops. The promise must be **stable**: created outside rendering (by a cache, a framework's data loader or a parent) or passed from a Server Component. A promise created in the same component's render is new every time and would suspend forever. Suspense does **not** detect data fetched in an effect.

Design notes:

- Place boundaries where a loading state makes sense to the user. Nested boundaries reveal content progressively, outer first.
- Siblings inside one boundary are revealed together, avoiding a jumpy one-by-one pop-in.
- When an update would hide already-visible content behind a fallback, wrap it in a **transition** (next lesson) and React keeps showing the old UI instead.
- Since React 19, when a component suspends, React shows the fallback immediately and then prepares the other components inside the boundary in the background ("pre-warming"), so the fallback isn't held up by rendering them.
takeaways: Suspense shows the nearest boundary's fallback while children are not ready
`lazy(() => import(...))` code-splits components; `use(promise)` reads promises during render
Promises passed to `use` must be stable (cached or created outside render)
pitfalls: Calling `use(fetch(url))` directly in render, creating a new promise every render.
Expecting Suspense to show a fallback for data fetched in a useEffect.

quiz.q: Which of these will make a Suspense boundary show its fallback?
options: A child rendering a lazy() component whose code hasn't loaded yet
A child that fetches data in useEffect and sets isLoading
A child that throws a regular Error
A child with a slow for-loop in render
quiz.explain: lazy components and use() on pending promises suspend; effects, errors and slow code do not trigger Suspense.

concepts.name: Transitions and useDeferredValue
concepts.summary: Mark updates as non-urgent with useTransition and startTransition, and let slow parts of the screen lag behind with useDeferredValue.
concepts.why: Transitions keep typing and clicking responsive during heavy renders and stop already-visible content flashing back to spinners.
takeaways: `startTransition(() => setX(...))` marks updates as interruptible, low priority
Transitions keep old UI visible instead of falling back to Suspense spinners
`useDeferredValue` gives a lagging copy of a value; pair it with a memoized slow child
pitfalls: Wrapping a controlled input's own state update in a transition, which makes typing lag.

quiz.q: A tab switch suspends while loading. Without a transition the whole panel shows a spinner. What does wrapping setTab in startTransition change?
options: The data loads faster
The Suspense fallback is shown sooner
React keeps showing the current tab until the new one is ready, with isPending true meanwhile
The update is applied immediately, blocking other work
quiz.explain: Transitions avoid hiding already-revealed content; React waits in the background and keeps the old UI interactive.

concepts.name: Error boundaries
concepts.summary: Catch errors thrown while rendering part of the tree, show a fallback with an error boundary, and report errors from the root.
concepts.why: Without error boundaries, one failing component removes the entire app from the screen and leaves users with a blank page.
concepts.body:
If a component throws during rendering, React can't produce a consistent UI, so by default it **unmounts the whole tree**. An **error boundary** limits the damage: it catches errors thrown while rendering its descendants (including errors in their Effects, and rejected promises read with `use`) and renders a fallback instead. Error boundaries are still written as **class components**: components written as a JavaScript class with a `render` method instead of as a function. This is the one place modern code needs them. A class becomes a boundary by defining `static getDerivedStateFromError(error)` (returns state to render the fallback) and optionally `componentDidCatch(error, info)` (to record the error, for example by sending it to a reporting service; `info.componentStack` shows which components it happened in). Most teams use the small **`react-error-boundary`** package instead of writing one: ```jsx Something went wrong.

}> ``` Error boundaries do **not** catch errors in event handlers (those don't happen during rendering; use try/catch and set state), in async code outside rendering (`setTimeout`, a fetch in a handler), or in the boundary itself. Placement is a design choice, like Suspense boundaries: one at the top as a last resort, plus finer ones around independent widgets (a sidebar, a chart, a route) so a failure in one doesn't take down the rest. Offer a way to try again: `react-error-boundary` gives the fallback a `resetErrorBoundary` function, and changing the boundary's `key` also remounts it fresh. React 19 also improves reporting: each error is printed once instead of several times, and `createRoot` accepts `onCaughtError` (errors a boundary caught), `onUncaughtError` and `onRecoverableError` options: the right place to send errors to an error-tracking service such as Sentry.
takeaways: Error boundaries catch render-time errors in their subtree and show a fallback
They're class components (`getDerivedStateFromError`); `react-error-boundary` wraps this nicely
They don't catch event-handler or unrelated async errors; use try/catch there
pitfalls: Expecting an error boundary to catch an exception thrown inside an onClick handler.

quiz.q: A button's onClick throws an error. The button is inside an error boundary. What happens?
options: The boundary shows its fallback
The whole app unmounts
React retries the click
The error propagates as a normal JavaScript error; the boundary doesn't catch it
quiz.explain: Event handlers run outside rendering, so error boundaries don't see their errors; handle them with try/catch.

concepts.name: Actions and form hooks
concepts.summary: Handle async mutations with Actions: form action props, useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic.
concepts.why: Actions are React 19's built-in answer to pending states, errors, optimistic updates and form resets that every app hand-rolled before.
takeaways: `<form action={fn}>` calls `fn(formData)` in a transition and resets the form on success
`useActionState` gives `[state, action, isPending]`; the action gets `(prevState, formData)`
`useFormStatus` reads the parent form's pending state; `useOptimistic` shows temporary UI
pitfalls: Calling `useFormStatus` in the same component that renders the `<form>`; it only reports on a parent form.

quiz.q: A form component calls useFormStatus() and renders <form action={save}>. Why is pending always false?
options: useFormStatus only works with Server Functions
useFormStatus reports on a form rendered above the calling component, not one it renders itself
The form needs an onSubmit handler too
pending is only true in production
quiz.explain: useFormStatus reads the nearest parent form's status; move the call into a child such as a SubmitButton.

quiz.q: What does the action passed to useActionState receive as its first argument?
options: The FormData
The submit event
The previous state
The isPending flag
quiz.explain: It is called as action(previousState, formData), so the first argument is the last returned state.

concepts.name: Fiber, lanes and concurrent rendering
concepts.summary: How React's Fiber design splits rendering into small units it can pause, ranks updates with lanes, and applies changes to the page all at once.
concepts.why: Concurrent features, Strict Mode's rules and many subtle bugs only make sense once you know how React schedules and discards work.
concepts.body:
