Internally, React represents your component tree as a linked tree of **fibers**: one object per component instance or page element (React calls the page's own elements "host" elements), holding its type, key, props, the list of Hooks (its state), links to its first `child`, next `sibling` and parent (called `return`), and flags describing pending DOM changes. Hooks state lives on the fiber, which is why Hooks are matched by call order.

React keeps two trees: the **current** tree (what's on screen) and a **work-in-progress** tree built from it, swapping them when done, like drawing the next page on a fresh sheet and then flipping it over. Rendering walks the work-in-progress tree one fiber at a time: `beginWork` calls the component and reconciles children, `completeWork` prepares host nodes and bubbles flags up. Because this is a plain loop over fibers, rather than functions calling themselves all the way down the tree (**recursion**), React can **pause** between fibers, let the browser handle clicks and drawing (it works in slices of a few milliseconds), and resume, or throw the work-in-progress away.

The **commit phase** is different: it's synchronous and can't be interrupted. React applies DOM mutations, attaches refs, runs `useLayoutEffect` callbacks (Effects that must run before the screen is redrawn) and swaps the trees, so users never see a half-updated UI. Ordinary Effects (`useEffect`) run afterwards.

Each update gets a **lane**: a priority level, stored as one bit of a number so React can combine and compare sets of lanes quickly. Discrete input (clicks, key presses) gets a sync lane, continuous events (scroll, mousemove) a higher-than-default lane, ordinary updates the default lane, `startTransition` updates transition lanes, and offscreen or idle work the lowest. A render handles a set of lanes; when a higher-priority update arrives during a transition render, React interrupts, handles the urgent lane, and later **restarts** the transition.

Consequences for your code: a render may run many times or never commit, so render must be pure and side effects belong in effects; reading mutable external data during render can produce **tearing** (different parts of one screen update showing different versions of the data), which is what `useSyncExternalStore` prevents. Sync updates are not interruptible, which is exactly why transitions exist.
takeaways: Each component instance is a fiber; Hook state lives on it as an ordered list
Render builds a work-in-progress tree in interruptible units; commit is synchronous and applied all at once
Lanes prioritise updates: input is sync, transitions are interruptible and can restart
pitfalls: Assuming every render is followed by a commit, e.g. counting renders or sending usage statistics from the component body.

quiz.q: Why must rendering be free of side effects in concurrent React?
options: Because React may start, pause, restart or abandon a render without committing it
Because the commit phase runs side effects twice
Because fibers are immutable
Because effects run before rendering
quiz.explain: Interruptible rendering means a render's result can be discarded; side effects in it would happen for UI that never appears.

quiz.q: Which part of an update can React interrupt to handle a more urgent update?
options: The commit phase
Rendering a transition's work-in-progress tree
Running useLayoutEffect
Applying DOM mutations
quiz.explain: Only the render phase of non-sync lanes is interruptible; commit is always synchronous.

concepts.name: External stores with useSyncExternalStore
concepts.summary: Subscribe to state that lives outside React safely, without tearing, using useSyncExternalStore.
concepts.why: State libraries, browser features and shared caches live outside React; reading them correctly matters once React can pause renders.
concepts.body:
Some state isn't owned by React: a Redux or Zustand store, `navigator.onLine`, `window.matchMedia`, a cache filled by a live server connection, `localStorage`. Such data is an **external store**. The naive approach (copy it into state in an effect and subscribe) causes a first render with out-of-date data, and, worse, **tearing** under concurrent rendering: if the store changes while React is rendering a transition in slices, components rendered before and after the change show different values in the same commit.

**`useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot?)`** solves this:

- `subscribe(callback)` registers a listener React calls whenever the store changes, and returns an unsubscribe function.
- `getSnapshot()` returns the current value. React calls it during render and checks it again before committing; if the value changed mid-render, React re-renders synchronously so the whole tree sees one consistent value.
- `getServerSnapshot()` returns the value to use when the page is rendered to HTML on the server (where browser features don't exist) and when React in the browser first takes that HTML over; without it, server rendering throws.

Rules that trip people up:

- `getSnapshot` must return the **same value** (by `Object.is`) when the store hasn't changed. Returning a new object or array each call (`{ ...state }`, `items.filter(...)`) causes an infinite loop. Return immutable snapshots and select or derive outside, or cache.
- Define `subscribe` outside the component (or memoize it); a new function each render re-subscribes every time.
- Updates to external stores are always urgent: they can't be marked as transitions, so a store change that suspends shows the fallback rather than keeping old UI.

This is the primitive state libraries build on; Redux's `useSelector` and Zustand's hooks are implemented with it. Wrap it in a custom Hook (`useOnlineStatus`) and components never know where the data lives.
takeaways: `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` reads external state without tearing
`getSnapshot` must return an identical value while the store is unchanged
Keep `subscribe` stable; external store updates can't be transitions
pitfalls: Returning a freshly built object or filtered array from getSnapshot, causing an infinite re-render loop.

quiz.q: Why does getSnapshot = () => store.items.filter(i => i.visible) cause problems?
options: filter is too slow for render
getSnapshot must be async
Arrays can't be stored in external stores
It returns a new array on every call, so React thinks the store always changed and re-renders endlessly
quiz.explain: React compares snapshots with Object.is; a new array each time never matches, triggering infinite updates.

quiz.q: What problem does useSyncExternalStore prevent that subscribing in useEffect does not?
options: Tearing: different components in one commit seeing different store values during concurrent rendering
Memory leaks from forgotten unsubscribe calls
Slow network requests
Hydration of class components
quiz.explain: React re-checks the snapshot before commit and forces a consistent synchronous render if it changed.

concepts.name: Server Components
concepts.summary: Run components on the server or at build time with React Server Components, and mark the interactive parts with 'use client'.
concepts.why: Server Components change where code runs: less JavaScript shipped, direct data access, and a new boundary every modern React developer must understand.
concepts.body:
**React Server Components (RSC)** are components that run only on the server (each time a page is requested) or when the app is built. Their code is never sent to the browser. They can be `async` and read data directly:

```jsx
export default async function Note({ id }) {
  const note = await db.notes.get(id);      // no API layer, no effect
  return <article>{note.body}</article>;
}
```

Their output is turned into a compact text format, the **RSC payload**, and sent to the browser, where React merges it into the page. They need special support from the bundler and server, so in practice you use them through a framework such as the Next.js App Router or React Router's RSC support. In such apps, components are Server Components **by default**.

Server Components can't use state, effects, event handlers or browser-only features. For interactivity you add **Client Components**: a module beginning with the `"use client"` directive marks a **boundary**; that module and everything it imports is bundled for the client (it is still turned into HTML on the server first, then comes alive in the browser). Composition rules:

- A Server Component can render Client Components and pass them **props that are serialisable**: strings, numbers, booleans, plain objects and arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, promises, JSX, and Server Functions. Not class instances or ordinary functions.
- A Client Component can't import a Server Component, but it can receive one as `children` or another JSX prop, so you can still nest server-rendered content inside client wrappers.
- Push `"use client"` down to the leaves (the button, not the page) to keep bundles small.

Server Components pair with Suspense: wrap a slow async component in `<Suspense>` and the rest of the page is sent first, with the slow part following when ready (**streaming**). You can also pass an unresolved promise to a Client Component and read it there with `use()`.

Keep **secrets** such as passwords and API keys on the server: import the `server-only` package in modules that hold them, and if one is ever pulled into browser code, the build fails.

Don't confuse Server Components with **server-side rendering** (SSR), which turns a component tree into HTML on the server so the first page appears quickly. Server Components decide which components run where; the two are used together.
takeaways: Server Components run on the server/at build, can be async, and ship no JavaScript
`"use client"` marks a boundary; props crossing it must be serialisable
Pass Server Components into Client Components as children; keep client boundaries at the leaves
pitfalls: Adding `"use client"` at the top of a page or layout, turning the whole subtree into client code.
Passing a function or class instance from a Server Component to a Client Component prop.

quiz.q: A Client Component needs to display a Server Component inside it. How is that done?
options: Import the Server Component inside the Client Component file
Add 'use server' to the Client Component
Have a Server Component parent render <ClientWrapper><ServerChild /></ClientWrapper>, passing it as children
It is impossible
quiz.explain: Client modules can't import server components, but they can render server-rendered JSX received as props such as children.

quiz.q: Which prop can a Server Component pass to a Client Component?
options: An onClick arrow function defined in the Server Component
A database connection object
A class instance with methods
A plain object { id: 1, title: 'Hi' }
quiz.explain: Props crossing the boundary must be serialisable; plain objects are fine, ordinary functions and class instances aren't.

concepts.name: Server Functions and server actions
concepts.summary: Call server code from the browser with 'use server' functions, use them as form actions, and secure each one like a public endpoint.
concepts.why: Server Functions replace hand-written API routes for mutations, but each one is a network endpoint with security implications.
concepts.body:
A **Server Function** is an async function marked with `"use server"` that runs on the server but can be called from the client. In the browser's code, the bundler replaces it with a small stand-in: calling that sends the arguments to the server, runs the real function there, and returns the result.

Define them either inline in a Server Component (with `"use server"` at the top of the function body) or in a module that starts with `"use server"`, whose exports all become Server Functions and can be imported by Client Components.

When a Server Function is passed to a form's `action` or called inside a transition, it's commonly called a **server action**. Combined with React 19's form features this is powerful:

```jsx
<form action={createNote}>       // works even before JavaScript has loaded
```

- `useActionState(serverFn, initial)` returns errors and results to the form; a third argument (the page's URL) lets the form work even before JavaScript loads. That is **progressive enhancement**: the plain HTML form works, and JavaScript makes it nicer.
- `useFormStatus` and `useOptimistic` work as with client Actions.
- After a change, you tell the framework which pages' server data is now out of date, so it renders them again (e.g. `revalidatePath` in Next.js).

Security is the main expert concern. Every Server Function is effectively a **public HTTP endpoint**: a web address anyone can send requests to. Anyone can call it with any arguments, regardless of whether your UI shows the button. So inside each function:

- Check **who** is calling (**authentication**: is there a logged-in session?) and **whether they may do this** (**authorization**: do they own this note?).
- **Validate** every argument, checking its shape and values (e.g. with the Zod library); `FormData` values are just strings anyone could have typed.
- Return only what the browser should see. Values an inline Server Function captures from its surroundings travel through the browser **encrypted** (scrambled), but still shouldn't include secrets.

Server Functions are designed for mutations; calls are handled one after another, so they're not a good tool for fetching data. Load data in Server Components instead.
takeaways: `"use server"` makes an async function callable from the client over the network
Pass Server Functions to `<form action>` or `useActionState` for progressive enhancement
Treat each one as a public endpoint: authenticate, authorise and validate every call
pitfalls: Relying on the UI hiding a button for security; anyone can invoke the Server Function directly.

quiz.q: A Server Function deleteNote(id) is only rendered for admins in the UI. Is it secure?
options: Yes, because the button is hidden for other users
No; any client can call it with any id, so it must check authorisation itself
Yes, because Server Functions can only be called from Server Components
No, because Server Functions run in the browser
quiz.explain: Server Functions are reachable network endpoints; hiding UI is not access control.

concepts.name: Hydration and streaming SSR
concepts.summary: Render pages to HTML on the server, send them in pieces with Suspense, and hydrate them in the browser without mismatches.
concepts.why: SSR shows content before JavaScript loads and lets search engines read pages; streaming and selective hydration keep it fast, and hydration mismatches are a classic bug in live apps.
concepts.body:
**Server-side rendering (SSR)** runs your components on the server to produce HTML, so users see content before JavaScript loads. The browser then **hydrates** the page (this step is called **hydration**): React renders the same tree in the browser and attaches event handlers and state to the existing DOM instead of recreating it. ```jsx // client entry hydrateRoot(document.getElementById("root"), ); ``` React's streaming APIs are `renderToPipeableStream` (Node.js streams) and `renderToReadableStream` (the browser-style Web Streams, for other server environments such as Deno, Bun and edge servers). With streaming, React sends the page's outer frame, the **shell**, immediately and leaves **Suspense** fallbacks where content isn't ready. As each boundary resolves on the server, React streams its HTML plus a tiny bit of JavaScript that swaps it into place, without waiting for the slowest data. Callbacks like `onShellReady` and `onShellError` let you set the status code and handle failures; `onAllReady` waits for everything (useful for search-engine crawlers, the programs that read pages to index them). To build pages ahead of time rather than per request, there are `prerender` APIs in `react-dom/static`. Hydration is also incremental. **Selective hydration** hydrates Suspense boundaries independently, and if the user clicks inside a boundary that isn't hydrated yet, React prioritises hydrating that one first. Hydration requires the client's first render to produce **exactly the same output** as the server. A **hydration mismatch** happens when it doesn't, typically from `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, `typeof window` checks, locale-dependent formatting, or invalid HTML nesting (a `
` inside a `

`) that the browser rewrote. React 19 prints one error showing what differed, then discards the server HTML up to the nearest Suspense boundary and renders that part on the client, losing the benefit of SSR there. Fixes: render client-only values in an effect after hydration, use `useId` for generated ids, and `suppressHydrationWarning` only for unavoidable one-element differences such as a displayed time. Frameworks wire all of this up; the concepts still decide where you put Suspense boundaries and why a page flickers.
takeaways: SSR renders HTML on the server; `hydrateRoot` attaches React to it on the client
Streaming sends the shell first and fills Suspense boundaries as data resolves
The first client render must match server HTML; avoid time, randomness and window checks in render
pitfalls: Rendering `new Date().toLocaleTimeString()` directly, so server and client output differ and hydration mismatches.

quiz.q: A component renders typeof window === 'undefined' ? 'Server' : 'Client'. What happens on hydration?
options: It shows 'Client' with no issues
The server throws an error
A hydration mismatch, because the client's first render differs from the server HTML
React skips hydrating this component
quiz.explain: The server rendered 'Server' but the client's first render produces 'Client'; render client-only content after an effect instead.

quiz.q: With streaming SSR, what does the browser receive first when one section is wrapped in Suspense and its data is slow?
